body_en_plain:
December, 1992     Page Reply


 How to write to us...02     -
 Francis Miles........03    13
 Mike Minchin.........21    29
 Les Tyler............32    38
 J. P. Messenbird.....39    41
 Bill Clark...........43    45

   PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE!
Text is accepted in any form for
OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files
(say which),typed or handwritten
letters. However, PLEASE send us
a textfile if possible so your
letter needn't be typed again!
The easiest for us to edit are
Tasword 2 files with the right
margin set at 32 but a textfile
in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be
parts of your letter you do not
wish published but we always use
our discretion anyway. Letters
may also be edited for clarity
and length... Please ask if you
welcome direct correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From: F.G. Miles, WELWYN

Dear Ron and Brian,

In your reply to Miles Kinloch's
letter in OUTLET 63 you suggest
that it's possible on the Spect-
rum 48K to SAVE and LOAD undim-
ensioned strings. This is true
enough but BEWARE!: you'll find
that although the string LOADs
back from tape or (I think)
Microdrive, you can't do any-
thing with the result.

 LET a$="hello"
 SAVE "message" DATA a$()
 LOAD "" DATA a$()

... all this is OK, but now
 PRINT a$
... produces "Subscript  wrong";

and so far I've not figured  out
a way of recovering the message.

You'll find more about this in
the ROM Index under 0605 SAVE
ETC (last paras before Input
Parameters). Bruce Gordon was
obviously alive to this fault
when he programmed the DISCiPLE/
PLUS D, which reject SAVEs of
undimensioned strings. ----

Some more miscellaneous comments
on OUTLET 63 - a specially good
Issue, it actually answers three
or four of my queries before
you'd published them!

OPENTYPE files (D. Burke, Brian
Gaff, Miles Kinloch): I've used
these in my assembler/disassem-
bler system (not yet finished,

though it works more or less) to
SAVE partly processed disassem-
blies on disc: the system uses
three different programs each
LOADing the product of the last.

The output stage of the semi-
disassembled code isn't kept in
a RAM buffer but pushed on to
disc as it's produced, so it
uses up very little memory: in-
deed stage 2 doesn't use a RAM
buffer at all, it inputs the
code line by line on one STREAM
and outputs it on another. Also
with OPENTYPE files you don't
need to know how long your code
is before you start SAVing it.

Thanks to Miles Kinloch for his
comments and program on the RAM
disc. I'll study this.

Thanks again to Miles Kinloch
for the PLUS D double-POKE.
Two comments on this:

1) Rather than use his suggested
DEF FN, surely it's simpler to
set a variable dp = 8192 and
then write POKE @ 50000-dp,2000
or whatever?

2) BEWARE! Programs with POKE @
aren't compatible even between
DISCiPLE and PLUS D: the dp for
DISCiPLE is 664. On DISCiPLE
this doesn't work if the POKEd
value is less than 256. Not sure
yet about PLUS D, I'll test it.

I'm amused to see the Slovak -
Esperanto - English translation
of SONG DEMO. I've been inter-
ested in Esperanto for years

but this is the first time I've
ever found it actually being
useful for anything. Some com-
ments (I sent you my own trans-
lation just before this ap-
peared):

BREAK starts the graphics again
but not the tunes

SS+SPACE saves the SCREEN$ on
tape

I think X means "reflection in-
visible"

R is "speed": it makes a prompt
with choice of speeds

Z was left out: it means "speed
of colour change"


Centrifugal force: This is an
old chestnut, and I've never yet
seen an explanation that wasn't
thoroughly muddling! If you are
holding a string and it pulls,
you naturally assume a force is
pulling it. When you're whirling
a stone on the end of the
string, this assumption is
wrong: it's you that is pulling,
if you didn't the stone would
fly off at a tangent.

A moving body will continue in a
straight line unless something
stops or deflects it: this is
Newton's First law. So you have
to pull the string, not to re-
sist a force but to keep the
stone from flying away. In this
sense, there is no "centrifugal
force" involved.

However, it sometimes helps in
calculations (eg when you're
working out how hard you must
pull the string for a given
weight of stone and speed of
whirl) to talk as if there were
such a force - and considering
the weird and imaginary entities
that physicists talk about all
the time, I'm blowed if I can
see any harm in it.

Is that better?

VAL$.

In the ROM Index under "VAL$
key" you'll find a sug- gested
use for it: a program which
handles and combines alge- braic
functions. Each function is
input as a string: eg.

LET f$ = "(x+7)"
LET g$ = "(x*4 + x*3)"

Then LET h$ = VAL$ """COS "" +
f$ + ""+ SIN"" + g$"

would produce the function

h$ = "COS (x+7)+ SIN(x*4 + x*3)"

(I think): and if you gave a
value to x in the ordinary way,
PRINT VAL h$ would give the
value of the function. But such
a program would be too hard for
me. Could the idea be used in
SOLVEX?

I'm now getting used to my re-
cently acquired PLUS D and two
disc drives. Some queries:

1) When I FORMAT a disc on drive
2 everything seems OK till I try
to SAVE @ sectors on it;then I
get a SECTOR ERROR, usually at
track 0 sector 2, and everything
on that disc is lost for ever.
Is this a common problem? Is
there a fault in my disc drive?

2) Does the PLUS D have a double
POKE similar to the DISCiPLE's
POKE @ xxxx-664,y? I've tried a
range of offsets (664 doesn't
work) but can't find the magic
number, if any.


3) If you're working with two
disc drives (with PLUS D) what's
the quickest way to switch from
one to the other?

 1. CAT 1 (or 2)
 2. LOAD @1 (or 2),0,0,65000
 3. LOAD d1 (or d2) "*"

- assuming you have "AUTOLOAD"
in p1 on the new disc.

All these work. I mostly use 3,
but 2 is obviously better as a
program line.

Presumably PLUS D has a system
variable holding the current
drive number - it ought to be
23766, like Microdrive, but this
doesn't always seem to work.

        Yours sincerely,

        FRANCIS G MILES

Brian Cavers to Francis Miles

The sector errors you get may be
due to incompatibility between
the two drives, i.e., calibrated
at opposite ends of the range of
tolerance. However,I suspect the
reason may be a problem with the
+D dos which arises in certain
situations, one of which may be
not because you formatted the
disc on drive 2 and tried to
SAVE to that disc in drive 1 but
because you had JUST used drive
2 and the system might take a
fraction longer to get to the
correct sector after a drive
switch and starting writing to
soon. This is just a vague hunch
but you might try using drive 1
(e.g., CAT 1) before the SAVE.

Another thing you could try is a
double SAVE @ as we find that
sometimes that works.

However, all this is very, very
unsatisfactory. We have had many
wierd problems including disc
corruption and I have suspected
it was poor connections corrupt-
ing the system. I have recently
ordered BETADOS from Andy Wright
of BetaSoft and his reply does
encourage my alternate suspicion
that it may be a G+ dos fault. I
have arranged for Chris Oliver
to test BETADOS and, if it cures
these problems, will order a
copy for myself and recommend it
to everyone else. These faults
are so intermittent though it
may take a month or two to prove
or disprove.

Yes, you can do a double poke on
the Plus D using...


         POKE @ xxx-8192

However, as mentioned before, I
do not recommend this method in
programs because it is incompat-
ible with other systems and is
relatively easy to set up a
routine to do the same on any
system. One never knows when one
might want to pass a program to
a friend or even send it in to a
disc magazine!

Nevertheless the POKE @ method
might be handy if one is experi-
menting, exploring or testing,
etc.

Regarding switching drives the
quickest way as a direct command
is CAT 1"""". Incidentally, your
LOAD @ has two errors: there is
no Sector 0 - it must be 1 to 10
and if the address is 65000 it
will overwrite the stack at its
normal default position of 65367
though I assume your values were
just off the top of your head!

Regarding a system variable for
the drive number, Malcolm Perry
explored and found...

 LOCATION    DISCIPLE     +D
              D1  D2    D1  D2

6862 (plus)    1   0     1   2
7642 (8192)   17  16     1   2
7681 (if+D)    1   2     1   2

Naturally,these cannot be PEEKed
unless you use a routine like
PEEK @ (OUTLET 43. PEEK @ works
only the Disciple though a handy
coder like yourself could easily
modify it by altering the IN 187
and OUT 187 which pages in the
Disciple ROM to a RST 8, DEFB 71
and OUT 231 respectively (plus
presumably alter offsets).By the
way,if you do, you might send in
the results! I've never had time
to convert it!


If 7642 is POKEd it will force a
drive change. On a Disciple this
is "immediate" but on a +D this
will only take effect when the
default drive is next used.

Regarding centrifugal force, I
still am not convinced because
it seems to me the tendency for
the movin object to continue in
a straight line and thereby move
away at a tangent to the spin
just DESCRIBES what centrifugal
force IS. That is, it explains
what the words mean but the
phenomenon still exists as an
experience.

I would further challenge that
the only force present is the
person pulling on the string
because it seems to me there are
TWO forces IN BALANCE. If there
were only one then movement
would take place as illustrated
if two people pull on opposite
ends of a rope with equal force
and then one lets go!

Indeed, as far as the pull is
concerned, you could not tell
the difference whether it was
caused by a person or an object
trying to continue in a straight
line. This indicates to me that
both must be classed as forces.

Just as you can analyse the pull
by the person as caused by a
chemical reaction in his muscles
so one can analyse centrifugal
force and see that it is caused
by Newton's law.

You should find centrifugal
force in any dictionary but does
anyone know of a reference work
in physics that describes it or
refutes its existence? Perhaps
its absence would indicate it is
not recognized scientifically!

Regarding your VAL$ use, is it
not true that one could simply
substitute LET h = VAL and drop
a couple of quotation marks? You
then simply PRINT h instead of
VAL h$.

                     A. Soandso


From: Mike Minchin, LONDON, SW14

At last I have got round to
reading OUTLET, Issues 59-63. (I
also run a PC clone which has
used up a lot of time recently).
For what it's worth, here are my
thoughts on some issues brought
up in your letters column. As it
helps your financial state, I'm
for the already announced price
increase for OUTLET. But, then,
I can afford it at the moment -
there were redundancies in my
work place in September, but I
survived (this time).

On the MasterDOS/BASIC discuss-
ion, they convert the SAM to
much more like what Andy Wright
must have hoped for the machine.
If you're into programming and

can afford them, then they are
an absolute must. If you can't
afford them, then they ought to
be at the top of your list of
things to save up for.

Viruses: I take care with my PC
clone, but I agree that the SAM
is unlikely to be afflicted,
primarily because the user base
is too small. I can think of a
way that a virus could be passed
from SAM to SAM, but no way am I
going to tell.

In OUTLET 63's Spectrum mail
there was a query about why line
numbers are held with the high
value byte first, contrary to
the usual Z80 convention. The
answer lies in a very important
routine at &19B8 called NEXT-ONE

by Dr. Ian Logan. This is used
whenever a particular line needs
to be found(GO SUB,GO TO,etc).OR
when searching for a variable.
The routine finds "the next
entry" which might be a line or
one of the 6 variable types the
Spectrum uses. The three high
bits of the first byte it looks
at tells NEXT-ONE which of the 7
possible methods it must use to
calculate the "next" address. As
the storage of variables is not
under the control of a BASIC
programmer, but the value of a
line number is, it was easiest
to limit line numbers to below
10000, place the high-value byte
first, and so make the line
identifier byte 000xxxxx. Oh,
yes. Why 9999 and not 16383 as
the highest line number?

Because it saves a few bytes in
the number printing routine at
&1A28 (a maximum of 4 digits)!
SAM stores variables in a very
different way from the Spectrum,
and so could not use an all-
purpose NEXT-ONE routine. Hence,
higher line numbers are allowed,
but they are still "the wrong
way round", so as to keep some
Spectrum compatability.

I notice that a number of your
Spectrum readers use the OCP
Assembler/editor. That was my
favourite Spectrum Assembler,
despite its willfully perverse
text editor, so you can imagine
my excitement when I discovered
a copy of the Microdrive + 80
column printer version.

You can also imagine my dis-
appointment, later, when I found
that running it on the "Micro-
drive compatible Disciple"
caused an Illegal Hook Code
error. I investigated the OCP
code. Your correspondent is
quite right - the program could
never run on any 128K Spectrum
because the Printer Buffer is in
constant use as a work space.

The reason for my crash was that
OCP (or Mr.Hutchby, if he had
amend- ed the code - though from
inter- nal evidence I would say
he did not) had added a routine
to test for the presence of the
Inter- face One in a way that
broke all the rules. To make it
legal on Interface One, +D, and
Disciple:

      POKE 38782,207  ; rst  8
      POKE 38783, 49  ; defb 31h
      POKE 38784,201  ; ret

With those 3 bytes changed, the
OCP Assembler/Editor causes a
Disciple/+D to produce type 8
(M/DRIVE) files. But beware -
these may only be read by those
interfaces. They take pains to
simulate a Microdrive channel,
when requested to do so from
machine code, but a "Microdrive
sector" of 512 data bytes, SAVEd
onto disc, also carries 28 bytes
of buffer data (twelve bytes of
which need never have been
included).

This is my first outing with
OUTWRITE! mark 2. Many improve-
ments on version 1, but it'll

take a bit of time to learn some
of them. I've already found a
bug: I tried to SAVE text onto a
write-protected disk. My wrist
was rightly slapped but when I'd
unprotected the disk the program
refused to accept that the error
condition no longer held, and I
had to BREAK and GO TO 50.

I'm afraid I disagree with you
as to what a "proper Insert
mode" is. It is what you call a
"character insert mode", not a
"line insert mode", and all Word
Processers written for business
machines agree with me. I'm also
not convinced that the Tasword
2/OUTWRITE! text format of a
constant 64 characters per line
and no Carriage Return (let
alone a Line Feed) is the best.

You will notice that I've given
you two copies of this 32 column
letter and that the variable
length line + CR version is
distinctly less than half the
size of the OUTWRITE! version.
Still, it is such a standard on
Spectrum and SAM that I suppose
you are lumbered with it. You
notice, though, that I still use
OUTWRITE!!

        Yours sincerely,

     Michael J.D.G. Minchin
             (Mike)

Brian Cavers to Mike Minchin

I tried to save text in OUTWRITE
onto a write-protected disc and,
like you, got the error prompt.
I then locked the disc tab and
tried again without any problem.

There is no bug in OUTWRITE in
this respect.How could there be?
It only uses the BASIC SAVE and
ON ERROR. I can only assume you
did not push the tab up fully on
the disc. If it is even slightly
down, it defaults to fail-safe
and you cannot write to a disc.
Try it again and double-check
you push the tab up fully. The
only other thing I can suggest
is that your DOS was corrupted
in some way.

Incidentally, I recommend that
you avoid using the BREAK button
if possible as it may corrupt
BASIC. In OUTWRITE, select USER
BASIC on the Options Menu.

I totally disagree with you when
you say a "proper insert mode...
...is a character insert mode".
This is just not true and a mis-
use of words. What you actually
mean is that a character insert
mode is the most common or most
standardised method. You also
say that "all business machines
agree with me". OUTWRITE was not
written for commercial use (but
it could be used by a small
business). OUTWRTIE is written
for a home computer for use in
the home.

If you want to say you prefer
one method to another then I'd
respect your point of view even
if I didn't share it but I just
cannot accept your statement
that a method that is less
common than another is thereby
"not proper". This is clearly
UNTRUE. Using your definition of
"proper" then the SAM Coupe is
not a "proper" computer and yet
it is!

Compare that with your statement
that "I'm also not convinced the
OUTWRITE text format is best".
Now, that I respect. It is a
legitimate point of view and you
are entitled to express it. Just
don't claim OUTWRITE does not
have a "proper" text format!
                     - Brian.

From: Les Tyler, CHELTENHAM

I thought I would put in a few
words concerning the many
excellent 128K music items
featured in recent months in
OUTLET. An enormous amount of
work has clearly gone into most
of these which have provided me
with a great deal of pleasure.
Many thanks to those concerned,
I hope to see plenty more of
their work!

The programs I like best are
those where the music is written
in the standard Spectrum format,
as with a very small amount of
modification these can be played
via the MIDI interface on the
128 through a keyboard, thereby
allowing a whole range of inst-

rumental sounds to be produced,
depending on the keyboard in
question. In May 1990 FORMAT
published an article by Frank
Kirby on connecting the 128K
Spectrum to a MIDI keyboard,
which I found to be perfect for
my requirements.

There was a reference in the
article to follow-up articles
but these have not materialised
for some reason or other, I
would like to know if Frank is
still around on the Spectrum
scene, as I would like to have
seen those follow-up articles.
Anyone who has a MIDI keyboard
and a 128K or +2 would find the
above article of great interest,
I am sure, as so much more can
be obtained from the musical

programs with the enhanced
sounds of the keyboard.

For example, Chris Ingram's
'Bach Fugues/Preludes' program
as scored on my Casio MT-750
with 4 channels, organ, oboe,
harpsichord and piano, sounds
superb!Similarly, J.E.Hutchings'
'Classic Guitar'gives a Segovia-
like result, especially when
string accompaniment is used for
the backing channels.

As there are 200 different tone
effects on this particular
keyboard, the range of sounds is
quite extensive, and each can
be altered at any time with the
flick of a switch, and made
permanent by minor alterations
to the BASIC program. Quite a

difference to the limited sounds
available through the Spectrum's
own system !

I also have a Yamaha PSS780 with
MIDI which can play up to 8
channels at once, however my own
personal preference is for the
CASIO as the sounds are rather
more authentic to my ears. Also,
the more channels, the more work
involved in utilising them, and
for the most part the 4 channels
of the CASIO are quite
sufficient for me.

If Frank is out there reading
this, or anyone knows him and
can pass on a message, I would
like to know something about how
he was going to program the
rhythm/accompaniment channels, I

have yet to sort that one out
satisfactorily. As regards the
other musical features in
OUTLET, I am very impressed by
those produced by our continent-
al colleagues, although the
actual musical style is rather
too modern for an oldie like me.

However, I am sure most red-
blooded males, irrespective of
age and musical tastes, enjoyed
the dancing girls in this
month's issue ! Anyone fancy
producing 'Swan Lake' complete
with ballerinas ? My own efforts
in producing music on Spectrum/
MIDI have been much more modest
than those of your contributors
so far, although I am working on
some bits that I hope will turn

into something of interest and
enjoyment to the readership....
watch this space !

As a matter of interest,
concerning your reference a
couple of issues ago to the
HOBBIT becoming available on the
UK market.I wrote to the address
you gave asking for information,
but have had no reply, has
anyone else made contact with
the firm in question?

           Les Tyler

Brian Cavers to Les Tyler

No, we have not received a reply
from the Hobbit people to our
inquiry either and I have heard
others report the same. I am not
inclined to do business with
organisations who cannot even be
bothered to answer a request for
their own product! It would not
hurt them to have a few hundred
photocopied slips saying what
the position is that they could
mail to all inquirers. Many have
sent SAEs as well.

It does seem to be the fashion
these days to ignore anything
but a cheque!
                        - Brian

From: J.P. Messenbird, MITCHAM

Dear Brian and Ron,

I am writing to say thank you to
everyone at CHEZRON SOFTWARE for
another brilliant edition of
OUTLET.

After recently changing my subs-
cription from tape to disk I am
finding how much more convenient
it is to use the disk version -
no more having to wind the tape
backwards and forwards - just
press the key and the program is
automatically loaded for you.

However, I am having problems
running the music programs on
the disk version of OUTLET. The
program starts to run and then

stops, with the message at the
bottom of the sscreen saying
"Nonsense in basic". Could you
help?

I would be glad to pay the new
price for OUTLET if it helps the
magazine's survival, it will be
very sad if OUTLET goes out of
business. `4.00 is still fant-
astic value for some of the best
Spectrum software around.

May I take this opportunity to
wish you a Merry Christmas and a
prosperous new year to OUTLET
and all its readers.

         Best wishes,

        J.P. Messenbird

Brian Cavers to J.P. Messenbird

Most of the music programs are
128K music and so need a 128K
Spectrum to work.Each one almost
always has a line that tests if
you have a 128K machine or a 48K
machine (or even if you are just
in 48K mode). If so, it displays
a message "SORRY! - 128K ONLY"
or similar. I can only think of
one way round this trap. You are
using the BREAK key to enter the
program and then entering RUN or
suchlike and directly going to
the PLAY command (which gives
"nonsense in BASIC" in 48K mode.
If not then please write again,
state the exact program, your
machine, what steps you took and
the line number of the error.

Another thought occurs to me. If
you have converted some of your
earlier tape versions of music
programs perhaps you saved them
on disc with the wrong autostart
line number (usually 8800) and
the programs immediately try to
use PLAY without the error-trap.

                       - Brian

From Bill Clark, FIFE

Dear Ron,

Some time ago I bought Tasprint
+3 for use with my Tasword +3
and could never get it to work.
I have written several times to
Tasman Software without reply. I
don't know if they are now out
of business!

I enclose two discs:one contain-
ing my working copy of Tasword
+3(customised for an Amstrad DMP
2000 printer) which works fine.
This disc also has a copy of the
basic Tasprint program (along
with instructions). The second
disc contains Tasword +3 with
Tasprint customised for the DMP
2000 - this DOESN'T work!!

The program seems to search for
the required fonts but will not
print out -just ignoring the new
fonts.

I would be grateful for your
help as I haven't a clue what to
do next.

I would finish by congratulating
you on the continuing high
standard of OUTLET magazine.
Keep up the good work!

Thanking you in antcipation.

          Bill Clark

Brian Cavers to Bill Clark


I found exactly the same but you
should by now have received your
discs back with my reply showing
that the fault lay with version
2.6 of Tasword +3 and that my
version 2.2 was O.K.!

                        - Brian.

## Letters (1)

December, 1992     Page Reply

How to write to us...02     - Francis Miles........03    13 Mike Minchin.........21    29 Les Tyler............32    38 J. P. Messenbird.....39    41 Bill Clark...........43    45

PLEASE SEND YOUR TEXTFILE! Text is accepted in any form for OUTLETTERS: wordprocessor files (say which),typed or handwritten letters. However, PLEASE send us a textfile if possible so your letter needn't be typed again! The easiest for us to edit are Tasword 2 files with the right margin set at 32 but a textfile in ANY format is appreciated!

Please state if there should be parts of your letter you do not wish published but we always use our discretion anyway. Letters may also be edited for clarity and length... Please ask if you welcome direct correspondence from other OUTLET readers and we will publish your full address.

From: F.G. Miles, WELWYN

Dear Ron and Brian,

In your reply to Miles Kinloch's letter in OUTLET 63 you suggest that it's possible on the Spect- rum 48K to SAVE and LOAD undim- ensioned strings. This is true enough but BEWARE!: you'll find that although the string LOADs back from tape or (I think) Microdrive, you can't do any- thing with the result.

LET a$="hello" SAVE "message" DATA a$() LOAD "" DATA a$()

... all this is OK, but now PRINT a$ ... produces "Subscript  wrong";

and so far I've not figured  out a way of recovering the message.

You'll find more about this in the ROM Index under 0605 SAVE ETC (last paras before Input Parameters). Bruce Gordon was obviously alive to this fault when he programmed the DISCiPLE/ PLUS D, which reject SAVEs of undimensioned strings. ----

Some more miscellaneous comments on OUTLET 63 - a specially good Issue, it actually answers three or four of my queries before you'd published them!

OPENTYPE files (D. Burke, Brian Gaff, Miles Kinloch): I've used these in my assembler/disassem- bler system (not yet finished,

though it works more or less) to SAVE partly processed disassem- blies on disc: the system uses three different programs each LOADing the product of the last.

The output stage of the semi- disassembled code isn't kept in a RAM buffer but pushed on to disc as it's produced, so it uses up very little memory: in- deed stage 2 doesn't use a RAM buffer at all, it inputs the code line by line on one STREAM and outputs it on another. In OUTLET 63's Spectrum mail there was a query about why line numbers are held with the high value byte first, contrary to the usual Z80 convention. The answer lies in a very important routine at &19B8 called NEXT-ONE

by Dr. Ian Logan. This is used whenever a particular line needs to be found(GO SUB,GO TO,etc).OR when searching for a variable. The routine finds "the next entry" which might be a line or one of the 6 variable types the Spectrum uses. The three high bits of the first byte it looks at tells NEXT-ONE which of the 7 possible methods it must use to calculate the "next" address. As the storage of variables is not under the control of a BASIC programmer, but the value of a line number is, it was easiest to limit line numbers to below 10000, place the high-value byte first, and so make the line identifier byte 000xxxxx. Oh, yes. Why 9999 and not 16383 as the highest line number?

Because it saves a few bytes in the number printing routine at &1A28 (a maximum of 4 digits)! SAM stores variables in a very different way from the Spectrum, and so could not use an all- purpose NEXT-ONE routine. В почте OUTLET 63 был вопрос о том, почему номера строк хранятся старшим байтом вперед, вопреки обычной практике Z80. Ответ кроется в очень важной подпрограмме по адресу &19B8, которую доктор Иэн Логан (Dr. Ian Logan) назвал NEXT-ONE. Она используется каждый раз, когда нужно найти определенную строку (GO SUB, GO TO и т.д.) ИЛИ при поиске переменной. Подпрограмма находит «следующий элемент», которым может быть либо строка, либо один из 6 типов переменных Спектрума. Три старших бита первого проверяемого байта сообщают NEXT-ONE, какой из 7 возможных методов следует использовать для вычисления адреса «следующего» элемента. Так как хранение переменных неподконтрольно программисту на Бейсике, а значение номера строки — подконтрольно, проще всего было ограничить номера строк значениями менее 10000, поместить старший байт первым и тем самым сделать идентификаторный байт строки равным 000xxxxx. Потому что это экономит несколько байт в подпрограмме печати чисел по адресу &1A28 (максимум 4 цифры)!
